passage: Rain was leaking through the classroom roof, so Miss had to hand back the maths tests from the one dry corner. Amandeep's paper had a wet blotch next to the red 9 out of 25. Jatin's was also a 9. Walking home under Jatin's small umbrella, their shoulders getting soaked, Amandeep kicked a puddle. 'I'm stupid. I'm always going to be stupid at maths.' Jatin was quiet for a bit. 'I didn't study that chapter,' he said. 'The fractions one. I was doing cricket all week.' At the gate, Jatin asked, 'Want to do fractions at my house tomorrow?' Amandeep shook his head. 'What's the use?' That evening Jatin sat under a dripping balcony with his book open. Amandeep folded his test into a tiny square and pushed it deep into his bag.

qa.q: What marks did both boys get on the maths test?
qa.a: Amandeep's paper had a red 9 out of 25, and Jatin's was also a 9.

qa.q: How can you tell Amandeep felt hopeless about maths?
qa.a: He said 'I'm always going to be stupid at maths', shook his head at Jatin's offer, and folded his test into a tiny square.

qa.q: What could Amandeep try the next time he gets a low mark?
qa.a: He could ask which chapter he didn't understand, like Jatin did, and join Jatin to practise fractions instead of saying 'What's the use?'

qa.q: How might Jatin feel when Amandeep says no to studying together?
qa.a: Jatin may feel a little disappointed, since he wanted to try again together and Amandeep has given up before starting.

grounding: Two boys with the same low mark explain it differently: one calls himself stupid for good and stops trying, the other blames an unstudied chapter and studies again.

passage: On the stairs of Building C, in their Mumbai colony, Farida and Nandini compared their Hindi test papers. Both had 11 out of 30. Nandini pointed at the red circles. 'I didn't study the poem chapter. I thought it wouldn't come.' Farida pulled her knees up. 'I'm stupid,' she said. 'I'm stupid in Hindi and I'll always be stupid in Hindi.' A pigeon landed on the railing and they both watched it. 'You got the grammar right,' Nandini said. 'So?' The next evening Nandini's Nani made her read the poem aloud three times on the same stairs. Farida walked past with her cycle and didn't stop. When Nandini called out, 'Come, we'll learn it together!' Farida just rang her bell and kept going.

qa.q: What marks did Farida and Nandini get in the Hindi test?
qa.a: Both had 11 out of 30.

qa.q: What does Farida pulling her knees up and saying 'I'm stupid' suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels ashamed and sure the problem is permanent, so there is no point trying.

qa.q: What could help Farida the next evening on the stairs?
qa.a: She could stop her cycle and learn the poem with Nandini, starting from the grammar she already got right.

qa.q: What is it like for Nandini when Farida rides past?
qa.a: Nandini wants to help Farida and learn together, so it may feel lonely and a bit worrying when Farida just rings her bell and keeps going.

grounding: Two girls get the same low mark; one says she is stupid and gives up, the other blames a skipped chapter and practises it.

passage:
'Chacha, don't look at my report card. I'm stupid.'
'Jatin, it's one test.'
'It's science. I'm stupid in science. I'll always be.'
'Hm. Gunjan, what did you get?'
'Same marks,' said Gunjan, not looking up from her rice. 'Twelve.'
'And are you stupid too?'
'No! I didn't study the magnets chapter. I spent the whole week on my dance practice.'
'So what happens next?'
'I'll do magnets on Sunday. Ramesh Chacha, will you check me?'
'If you let me eat first.'
Jatin pushed his dal around. 'She's just lucky.'
'Lucky with twelve?' said Ramesh Chacha. 'Jatin, which part did you get wrong?'
'All of it.'
'All of it? Let's see.'
Jatin didn't move. After dinner Gunjan spread her book on the floor. Jatin went to his room and shut the door.

qa.q: Which chapter did Gunjan say she didn't study?
qa.a: Gunjan said she didn't study the magnets chapter.

qa.q: What was Jatin feeling when he said 'She's just lucky'?
qa.a: He seemed discouraged and defensive, as if Gunjan's plan made his own giving up feel worse, so he explained her calm as luck.

qa.q: What small step could Jatin take after dinner?
qa.a: He could show Ramesh Chacha the test so they can find the specific parts he got wrong, instead of deciding it was all of it.

qa.q: How does Ramesh Chacha see Jatin's words 'All of it'?
qa.a: Ramesh Chacha doesn't accept that it is all wrong and wants to check the paper, seeing the problem as something specific and fixable.

grounding: Two children with the same low science mark explain it differently at dinner, one as being stupid and one as an unstudied chapter, and only the second plans to try again.

passage: I'm Divyansh. Last month Harish and I both failed the geography test. We got 8 out of 25 each. On the bus I tore mine into little bits and said, "I'm stupid. I'll always be stupid at maps." Harish just looked at his paper. "I didn't learn the rivers chapter. That's all the questions." Then he folded it into his bag. That week he learnt the rivers with his sister. I didn't open the book, because what was the point? In the next test Harish got 19. I got 9. Now, when I'm stuck, I try saying "I didn't learn it yet." It feels less heavy.

qa.q: What did Harish say about the rivers chapter?
qa.a: "I didn't learn the rivers chapter. That's all the questions."

qa.q: Why did Divyansh tear the test into little bits on the bus?
qa.a: Divyansh felt ashamed and hopeless, sure of being "stupid at maps" forever, so the paper felt like proof.

qa.q: Which way of explaining the bad mark worked better, and why?
qa.a: Harish's, because blaming one unlearnt chapter pointed to something fixable, so he studied the rivers and got 19 next time.

qa.q: What would change if Divyansh had explained the mark the way Harish did?
qa.a: Divyansh might have opened the book that week instead of giving up, and the next mark could have looked more like 19 than 9.

grounding: Two children fail the same test; one decides they are stupid and stops trying, while the other blames an unlearnt chapter and studies it.

passage:
Tuition teacher's note, Class 6 batch, Friday.
Today I returned the fractions test. Vasudha and Sachin both scored 6 out of 20. Sachin frowned and said, "I didn't do the word problems at home. I'll do them this weekend." Vasudha pushed her paper away. "I'm just dumb at maths. I always will be." She would not pick up her pencil for the rest of the hour. After class I sat with her and asked her to circle every mistake. All of them were in the word problems; the sums she had practised were right. I asked, "So which is it, dumb at maths, or haven't practised these yet?" She was quiet a while, then said, "Haven't practised these." I have given her five word problems for Monday and will check them with her first.

qa.q: What did Vasudha and Sachin each score?
qa.a: 6 out of 20.

qa.q: Why wouldn't Vasudha pick up her pencil for the rest of the hour?
qa.a: She explained the bad mark as permanent, being "just dumb at maths", so trying again felt pointless to her.

qa.q: Why did asking Vasudha to circle every mistake help?
qa.a: It showed every mistake was in the word problems, turning "dumb at maths" into a specific gap she could practise.

qa.q: How might Sachin's weekend differ from Vasudha's, given how each explained the mark?
qa.a: Sachin saw a temporary cause and had a clear task for the weekend; Vasudha, before the teacher's help, had only a heavy belief about herself.

grounding: Two children fail the same test; one calls it a permanent flaw and stops, the other blames missing practice and plans to fix it.

passage:
Monday: The maths test came back. Abhinav had 9 out of 25 and Pradeep had 8. Abhinav crumpled his paper. "I'm stupid at maths. Always will be." Pradeep frowned at his. "I didn't do the fractions chapter. That's why."
Wednesday: Miss announced a retest on Friday. Pradeep practised fractions at recess, muttering under his breath. Abhinav drew cricket bats on his rough page. "Why bother? I'll fail again."
Friday: Pradeep got 17. Abhinav got 10 and stared out of the window. "Told you," he said. Pradeep pushed his rough page across. "Try the fractions ones with me tomorrow. That's the part you missed too."

qa.q: What mark did Pradeep get on Friday?
qa.a: Pradeep got 17.

qa.q: What was Abhinav feeling when he said "Why bother? I'll fail again"?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and discouraged, sure that being "stupid at maths" could never change.

qa.q: What could help Abhinav try again?
qa.a: Seeing the problem as one chapter rather than himself, and practising fractions with Pradeep as offered.

qa.q: How does Pradeep's explanation of his low mark change what he does?
qa.a: Because Pradeep blamed a chapter he skipped, the problem felt fixable, so he practised and improved.

grounding: Shows two children explaining the same bad test differently, one as a permanent flaw and one as a missed chapter, and how that shapes whether they try again.

passage:
Arre, one bad test and your face looks like a burnt roti? Listen. When I was in class four in Lucknow, your Dilnaz Nani failed the dictation test. So did my best friend Aditi. I cried under the neem tree and told her, "I am stupid. I'll never learn spellings."
Aditi wiped her nose and said, "I didn't practise the long words, that's all." Every evening that week she wrote ten hard words on her slate. I didn't. Why bother, if I was stupid?
Next test, she got nearly all of them right. I failed again, and believed it even more. Only in class six, when a teacher made me practise with Aditi, did I learn I wasn't stupid. I was unpractised. Now, which chapter did you skip?

qa.q: Where did Dilnaz cry after failing the dictation test?
qa.a: Under the neem tree.

qa.q: How did young Dilnaz feel after the failed dictation?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and hopeless, believing she was stupid and could never learn spellings.

qa.q: What choice in the story made Aditi's next test go better?
qa.a: Aditi blamed the unpractised long words, not herself, so she wrote ten hard words on her slate each evening.

qa.q: How did Aditi see the same failed test?
qa.a: As a temporary gap in practice she could fix, not a sign that she was stupid.

grounding: A grandmother recalls how she and a friend explained the same failed test, one as being stupid and one as lack of practice, and how that shaped their next try.

passage:
The inter-house science quiz ended badly: Irawati's team scored 2, Sabina's scored 3, both last. In the auto home, Irawati pressed her face to the window. "I'm just dumb. Science isn't for me." Sabina counted on her fingers. "We lost on the planets round. We never read that chapter."
The rematch was the next morning, and that evening the power went out in their lane. Sabina came over with a torch and the textbook. "Planets only. Forty minutes." Irawati lay on the bed. "What's the point?"
But Sabina read aloud anyway, and after a while Irawati sat up and asked, "Wait, which one has the rings?"

qa.q: Which round did Sabina say they lost on?
qa.a: The planets round.

qa.q: What was Irawati feeling in the auto home?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and defeated, seeing the loss as proof she was "just dumb" at science.

qa.q: What made Sabina's plan workable despite the power cut?
qa.a: Sabina shrank the fix to one chapter and forty minutes and brought a torch, so trying felt small enough to do.

qa.q: What would change for Irawati if she explained the loss the way Sabina did?
qa.a: She would see it as one unread chapter she could fix, and would be more likely to keep trying.

grounding: Shows two children explaining a quiz loss as either a permanent lack of ability or a missed chapter, and how the second view leads to trying again.

passage:
In the Pune school corridor, Vasudha and Rashmi got back their science tests. Both had four out of twenty.
Vasudha crumpled hers. "I'm stupid. I'm always going to be bad at science."
Rashmi looked at hers and frowned. "I didn't study the magnets chapter. That's where I lost all the marks."
"Same for me," said Vasudha. "But I'm just stupid."
"You're not. You just didn't study magnets either."
The next week, Rashmi borrowed a magnets book from the library. Vasudha didn't open her science notebook at all. "What's the point?" she said.

qa.a: Both had four out of twenty.

qa.q: What was Vasudha feeling when she crumpled her test?

qa.q: What could help Vasudha try again?

qa.q: How does Rashmi explain her own low mark?
qa.a: Rashmi explains it as not studying the magnets chapter, a temporary cause she can fix, so she borrows a book.

grounding: Shows two children with the same low mark explaining it differently, one as permanent stupidity, the other as a chapter not studied, and trying again or giving up.

passage:
In Class 6, I failed the Hindi dictation. I'm Anand. I remember going home and telling myself, "I'm useless at Hindi. I always will be."
My classmate Vasudha had failed too. She shrugged and said, "I didn't learn those new words. Next time I will."
For the next month, I stopped trying in Hindi class. I didn't even look at the words. Why bother if I'm useless?
Vasudha made little word cards and practised on the bus. The next dictation, she got fifteen out of twenty. I got five.
It took me years to see the difference wasn't talent. It was how we explained that first bad day.

qa.q: What did Vasudha make to practise the words?
qa.a: She made little word cards.

qa.q: How did Anand feel after failing the dictation?
qa.a: Anand felt hopeless and useless, believing it would always be that way.

qa.q: What could Anand have said after that first bad day?
qa.a: Anand could have said the new words hadn't been learnt yet, and made a plan to practise, like Vasudha.

qa.q: How did Vasudha see her own failure?
qa.a: Vasudha saw it as temporary and fixable, caused by not learning the new words, so she kept trying.

grounding: Shows two children explaining the same failed test differently, one as permanent, one as temporary, and how it shaped whether they tried again.

passage: Class 4 note, monsoon week. The spelling test came back today, and both Tushar and Sunaina failed it. Rain was hammering on the windows. Tushar put his head down and said, "I'm stupid. I'm always stupid at spellings." He didn't open his book again. Sunaina frowned at her paper and said, "I didn't learn the second page. I thought it wasn't in the test." She started copying the words she'd missed. What I did next: I sat with Tushar and showed him that he got every word right from the first page. "So what happened with the second page?" He thought. "I didn't practise those." "That's something you can fix." He picked his pencil up again, slowly.

qa.q: What did Sunaina say she didn't learn?
qa.a: The second page.

qa.q: What was Tushar feeling when he put his head down?
qa.a: He felt discouraged and ashamed, believing he is always stupid at spellings.

qa.q: What did the note-writer do to help Tushar try again?
qa.a: Showed him he got the first page right and helped him see that not practising the second page was fixable.

qa.q: How might Sunaina's reaction differ from Tushar's?
qa.a: Sunaina saw the failure as a temporary cause, so she felt it could be fixed and started practising straight away.

grounding: Illustrates two children explaining the same failure as permanent or temporary, and how that shapes whether they try again.

passage:
Wednesday, in Ramzan
Today I got four out of fifteen in the maths test. I wanted to cry. I thought, I'm just stupid at maths. I'll never get it. At iftar I didn't even want dates. But Elizabeth failed too, and at break she just said, "Well, I didn't study fractions. I'll do that chapter this weekend." She wasn't even sad. And I thought, wait. I didn't study fractions either. We were at Nani's all Saturday. Maybe it's not that I'm stupid. Maybe it's just fractions I haven't done yet. Tomorrow I'll ask Abbu to help me with them after iftar. I feel a bit better now.
Noor

qa.q: What score did Noor get in the maths test?
qa.a: Four out of fifteen.

qa.q: How did Noor's feelings change after talking to Elizabeth?
qa.a: Noor went from feeling hopeless and stupid to feeling a bit better, seeing the failure as fixable.

qa.q: What is Noor's plan, and why is it a good one?
qa.a: Asking Abbu for help with fractions after iftar, because it targets the actual cause of the low mark.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth's way of explaining the failure help her?
qa.a: Seeing it as an unstudied chapter lets Elizabeth stay calm and try again that weekend.

grounding: Shows a child moving from "I'm stupid" to "I didn't study that chapter" after seeing a friend's explanation.

passage: It was harvest season, and half the village school had been helping in the fields. When the test papers came back, Noor and Nilesh had both failed the sums. Nilesh crumpled his paper and threw it in the ditch on the way home. "My head's made of mud. Baba says so too." Noor, walking beside him with her sister, looked at her own red marks. "We missed the whole week of division. We were cutting paddy." "So?" "So we just don't know division yet. We're not mud." Her sister said, "Master stays after school on Thursdays." On Thursday, Noor stayed. Nilesh walked past the classroom window, slowed down, then kept going.

qa.q: What did Nilesh do with his paper?
qa.a: He crumpled it and threw it in the ditch on the way home.

qa.q: How was Nilesh feeling when he said his head was made of mud?
qa.a: He felt hopeless and ashamed, believing he was permanently bad at sums.

qa.q: What could help Nilesh try again, as Noor did?
qa.a: He could see the failure as missing a week of division, not a mud head, and stay back for Master's Thursday help.

qa.q: How does Noor's sister react to the failed sums?
qa.a: She stays practical and encouraging, telling them about Master's Thursday help after school.

grounding: Illustrates two children explaining the same failure as permanent or temporary, and who tries again as a result.

passage: The week before Sinterklaas, Mr. Visser handed back the fractions test while everyone was still chattering about chocolate letters. Yuki saw 4 out of 10 in red and folded the paper into a tiny square. 'I am stupid,' she whispered to Jamal. 'I'm just bad at maths. I always will be.' Jamal had 5. He frowned at it, then shrugged. 'I didn't study the dividing part. I spent all Sunday on my Sinterklaas poem.' When Mr. Visser said anyone could take a retest on Friday, Jamal went up at break and asked for the practice sheet. Yuki stayed at her desk, pressing the folded square flat with her thumb. 'What's the point?' she said. Jamal came back and put a second practice sheet on her desk anyway.

qa.q: What mark did Yuki get on the fractions test?
qa.a: Yuki got 4 out of 10.

qa.q: What does Yuki folding the test into a tiny square suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: She seems ashamed and hopeless, as if the mark proves she is stupid for good, so she wants to hide it rather than fix it 😔

qa.q: What could help Yuki see the test the way Jamal does?
qa.a: Someone could ask her which part she got wrong and whether she studied it; tying the mark to one chapter makes it something she can change before Friday's retest.

qa.q: Why might Jamal react so differently to almost the same mark?
qa.a: Jamal explains it with a temporary reason, the dividing part he skipped, so trying again makes sense; Yuki explains it as permanent, so trying feels pointless.

grounding: Shows two children explaining the same setback as permanent or temporary, and how that decides whether they try again.
